title: Mangrove restoration at ecologically meaningful scale
bottleneck: Mangroves protect coasts, nurture fisheries, and bury carbon, but restoration efforts plant the wrong species in the wrong tidal zones so often that global success rates are dismal — many projects report survival below 30 percent. Monoculture plantings of convenient species replace diverse forests with fragile ones, and restored sites are frequently re-cleared for aquaculture. The science of hydrological restoration that actually works is known but rarely applied.
why_it_blocks: Coastal communities face rising seas and storm surge with mangroves as their cheapest defense; failed restoration wastes the narrow window to rebuild it. Every failed planting also burns political capital for conservation.
current_state: Evidence-based guidelines emphasizing natural hydrological restoration over mass planting are gaining traction, and community-led projects show far higher survival. But funding still rewards hectares planted — an input metric — rather than functioning forest, perpetuating the failure mode.
